job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our science lab, we explored how charges behave. First, we rubbed a plastic scale with a dry cloth. This process does not create new charges; instead, it simply transfers existing electrons from the cloth to the scale, leaving the scale negatively charged. When we brought this scale near tiny bits of paper, they were attracted to it. However, when we brought two similarly charged scales near each other, they pushed away, proving that like charges repel. Next, we discussed the Earth's structure. We learned that the crust is not one solid piece but is fragmented into massive tectonic plates that move slowly over the semi-molten mantle, not a sea of liquid lava. These plates are distinct from the continents themselves, which are just the land masses resting on top of these shifting slabs. Finally, we looked at lightning. It is not a form of fire or burning gas, but a massive electric discharge caused by the buildup of static charges in clouds. To protect buildings, we install a lightning conductor, which provides a safe path for the current to reach the ground, rather than pulling the strike toward the building. We also studied seismographs, which record the vibrations of past earthquakes to help us understand their intensity, though they cannot predict the exact timing of future tremors.

items.evidence: This process does not create new charges; instead, it simply transfers existing electrons from the cloth to the scale, leaving the scale negatively charged.
items.q: A plastic scale turns negatively charged after rubbing with a cloth. Where did its extra charge come from?
options: Electrons already in the cloth moved onto it
The rubbing made new electrons inside it
Electrons moved from it onto the cloth
Electrons came from the bits of paper
items.explain: Rubbing only transfers electrons that already exist, from the cloth to the scale; it creates no new charges.

wrong.why: reverses the direction of electron transfer
picks a nearby object from the experiment

items.evidence: However, when we brought two similarly charged scales near each other, they pushed away, proving that like charges repel.
items.q: Two scales are rubbed with the same cloth and brought close. What will you see?
options: They push away from each other
They pull toward each other
Nothing happens, as only paper is affected
They lose their charge at once
items.explain: Scales with the same kind of charge push apart, because like charges repel.

wrong.why: thinks charges only act on light things
thinks charge vanishes when objects meet

items.evidence: These plates are distinct from the continents themselves, which are just the land masses resting on top of these shifting slabs.
items.q: A student says continents and tectonic plates are the same thing. Why is that wrong?
options: Continents are land resting on top of the plates
Plates are only the land that lies above sea
Plates float on a sea of liquid lava
Continents are slabs that move over the mantle
items.explain: Continents are just land masses sitting on top of the moving plates, so the two are different.

wrong.why: thinks plates are the visible continents
thinks plates float on liquid lava
swaps the roles of plates and continents

items.evidence: To protect buildings, we install a lightning conductor, which provides a safe path for the current to reach the ground, rather than pulling the strike toward the building.
items.q: How does a lightning conductor protect a tall building?
options: It gives the current an easy path to the ground
It pulls lightning here so other places are safe
It burns the lightning gas before it lands
It stops clouds from building up any charge
items.explain: The conductor gives the electric current a safe path to the ground; it does not attract the strike.

wrong.why: thinks it acts on the clouds themselves

items.evidence: We also studied seismographs, which record the vibrations of past earthquakes to help us understand their intensity, though they cannot predict the exact timing of future tremors.
items.q: What can a seismograph's records help scientists do?
options: Judge how strong past quakes were
Tell the exact day of the next one
Stop the plates from moving further
Find which continent will shake next
items.explain: Seismographs record vibrations of past earthquakes to show their intensity, but cannot predict when the next one comes.

wrong.why: thinks recording an earthquake can stop it
mixes continents with plates and prediction
